title: A sequence of 131,072 items, each with an anchor name, where all the names have the same 32-bit FNV-1a hash
notes: The input is valid: a block sequence of 131,072 items `- &NAME 1`, and every NAME is different (section 3.2.2.2 allows any anchor name of non-space characters except flow indicators; section 6.9.2, production 102). The names are 85 characters long, built in 17 stages: each stage appends one of two 5-character blocks that leave the 32-bit FNV-1a hash in the same state, so every one of the 2^17 combinations has the same hash (a multicollision, found by a birthday search per stage; the blocks are in case.json and use only letters and digits). A reader that keeps anchor names in a hash table keyed by that hash, or by its low bits, puts all of them in one chain, and looking up or inserting each name then costs work that grows with the number of names already stored: 131,072 names are about 8.6 billion probes. The answer is the sequence of 131,072 ones, or a limit error. A reader with another hash function, a tree or a sorted list is not affected, and the case then only checks that it answers in bounded time. The time limit is 100 seconds and is a hang guard, not a measure of cost: a reader whose work grows with the square of the names takes longer than a linear one, but one that finishes inside the limit passes, so this case catches only a reader that hangs. It is not made larger to catch more: a reader that compares each name with the names before it, reading up to the first byte that differs, needs 1.4 times the limit only at 524,288 names, an input of 53 megabytes, and at that size six of the twelve libraries that can run the case, all reading in linear time, pass the 1024 megabyte memory bound. The bounds are the robustness requirement of the kit, not a rule of the specification. The input (about 12 MB) is generated from the product part of the recipe in case.json (docs/case-format.md); the expected result is `[[1, 1, ...]]`, stored without spaces to stay under the size a stored file may have. Fast mode leaves this case out (tag `slow`).

provenance.reference: Anchor names chosen to share one 32-bit FNV-1a hash, against an anchor table that placed names by that unseeded hash, so loading them took quadratic time.
